title: George Washington Never Had Wooden Teeth #shorts
description:
George Washington's wooden teeth are one of America's favourite myths. There was no wood.

By 1789 he had just one natural tooth left, so he wore dentures made of hippopotamus ivory, cow and horse teeth, metal springs, lead — and human teeth, some of them bought from enslaved people at Mount Vernon. The springs pushed his jaws apart, which is why he clamped his mouth shut. Old ivory stains and cracks, and can look like wood grain.

Animated, voiced and scored in code. Narration is a synthetic (text-to-speech) voice.

title: Paul Revere Never Shouted "The British Are Coming" #shorts
description:
On the night of April 18, 1775, Paul Revere did not gallop through the streets yelling "The British are coming!"

The ride was a secret mission, British patrols were out, and most colonists still considered themselves British. By his own and other accounts, the warning was closer to "The Regulars are coming out." He wasn't alone either: William Dawes also rode, Revere was captured before reaching Concord, and Samuel Prescott got through. Longfellow's 1861 poem made Revere the hero and left the others out.

Animated, voiced and scored in code. Narration is a synthetic (text-to-speech) voice.

title: Real Ninjas Probably Didn't Wear Black #shorts
description:
The black ninja suit is probably a theatre invention.

Historical ninja, or shinobi, were spies, and a spy's job is to blend in — so they disguised themselves as farmers, merchants and monks, and old ninja manuals describe those disguises. The all-black look likely comes from kabuki theatre, where stagehands dressed in black and the audience treated them as invisible; dressing a stage ninja the same way was the perfect trick. Prints and movies copied it.

title: Pirates Almost Never Made People Walk the Plank #shorts
description:
Walking the plank is the most famous pirate punishment — and it almost never happened.

Pirates wanted ships and cargo, and most crews simply surrendered. If a pirate wanted someone gone, they'd throw them overboard or maroon them on an island. There are a few reports of plank walks, mostly from the 1800s, after the golden age of piracy had ended. Stories, illustrations and then Peter Pan made the plank famous.
